item.page_text:
First shortwave and thermal infrared views complete the picture from the satellite’s three main instruments
The coast of north-west Australia, where the Indian Ocean meets desert and savannah, leads the first set of preliminary thermal infrared images released from Copernicus Sentinel-3C . Captured by the satellite’s Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer (SLSTR), the image shows warm coastal waters, eddies further out to sea, and land already hot in the morning sun.
Other images in the first batch detail cold waters and sea ice between Greenland and Iceland, and signatures of wildfires burning on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi.
“SLSTR’s thermal channels read temperatures to within a few tenths of a degree,” said Milen Tahtadjiev, Copernicus Sentinel-3 Mission Manager at EUMETSAT. “That precision is crucial for the forecast models that Europe’s weather services rely on, and for climate monitoring, including El Niño, marine heatwaves and long-term ocean warming. SLSTR data also show civil protection authorities where wildfires are burning and how fiercely, as in southern Europe this summer. With these incredible first images, we can be confident its measurements will keep supporting essential services for many years to come.”
SLSTR measures sunlight reflected from Earth in visible and shortwave infrared light, as well as thermal infrared, the heat that every surface gives off, even ice. This heat is invisible to the human eye, but it can reveal the temperature of the sea, land, ice and cloud tops day and night. The instrument also supports the detection of wildfires and their smoke within hours of each satellite pass, with EUMETSAT’s fire products the most downloaded Sentinel-3 products in its Data Store in 2025.
The shortwave and thermal infrared images follow SLSTR’s first image in visible light and the first observations from the satellite’s two other main instruments, the Ocean and Land Colour Instrument and the Synthetic Aperture Radar Altimeter.
North-west Australia on 4 November 2026 at 01:34 UTC (09:34 local time), seen in two views by the SLSTR instrument on Sentinel-3C. The coast of Western Australia runs from the Pilbara at the bottom left, past the deep inlet of King Sound and along the Kimberley at the top right, a vast region of tropical savannah.
In the shortwave infrared view, sunlight is reflected by the surface, showing red desert soil, darker vegetated ground in the Kimberley, blue sea and bright clouds. Over the ocean this view shows little detail, apart from the coast and reefs. The shortwave infrared channels are very sensitive not only to the intense heat from fires, but also to burned areas left after fires are extinguished. That morning there were dozens of active fires scattered across the Kimberley.
It is in the thermal infrared that the ocean really comes alive. The warm, shallow water of the North West Shelf glows almost white along the coast, while the open Indian Ocean is a few degrees colder. Swirls, filaments and “horsehead” shapes show where colder water carried north by the West Australian Current mixes with the warmer South Equatorial Current. Shapes like these form where faster-moving water meets slower-moving water. North-west of King Sound there are sets of parallel, arc-shaped ripples a few kilometres apart. These are internal gravity waves. They may be in the ocean, as the North West Shelf is one of the world’s hotspots for such waves, which form where strong tides push water over the edge of the shelf.
The images were taken during one of the strongest El Niño events on record. In northern Australia, fire danger is greatest late in the dry season, and in El Niño years the rains usually come later. The hot, humid pre-monsoon months known as “the build-up” then last longer.
Surface temperature of the sea and sea ice between Greenland, at the top and left, and Iceland, at the bottom, on 31 October 2026. Intricate patterns of cold water reach the icy coast of Greenland, where the sea freezes inside the fjords. Further north, the dark blue patches are sea ice, far colder than the water around it. The temperature at the surface of the ice, and of any snow lying on it, governs the exchange of heat with the atmosphere and drives the growth and melt of sea ice, so these measurements help scientists to follow the rapid warming of the polar regions.
SLSTR looks at each part of the surface twice, once straight down and once looking back through more of the atmosphere. This “dual view” is what makes its sea and sea-ice temperatures so accurate. The image is derived from thermal infrared measurements and includes sea-ice surface temperature, a product that EUMETSAT introduced earlier this year.
Hotspots detected over the Indonesian island of Sulawesi on 31 October 2026 by one of the SLSTR instrument’s fire channels. Each square marks a spot much hotter than its surroundings, most likely an active fire, and its colour shows the temperature measured. Actively burning fires cover only a small part of SLSTR’s thermal infrared pixels, which are 1km across. Smoke is visible as hazy, pale blue colours above the typically dark blue ocean. The hotspots shown here are among Sentinel-3C’s first fire signals. El Niño typically brings drought to Indonesia, and during the current event the country has been hit by wildfires that degrade vegetation and air quality.
Launched on 15 September 2026, Copernicus Sentinel-3C is a third satellite in the Copernicus Sentinel-3 constellation, which observes Earth’s oceans, as well as land, ice and atmosphere. The groundbreaking Sentinel-3 series began in 2016 and its data cover the entire planet and can reach users within three hours of collection. The new satellite will ensure these vital data streams continue well into the 2030s. Once commissioning is complete, Sentinel-3C will take over from Sentinel-3A, while some Sentinel-3A observation capabilities will remain in operations.

Nov 19 (Reuters) - Traffic was temporarily suspended over the Crimean Bridge ‌after an attack, Sergei Aksyonov, ‌Crimea's Russian-installed governor, said on Telegram on ​Thursday, adding that assessment of the damage was underway.
The attack is the third this week on the ‌bridge that connects ⁠mainland Russia with Crimea, which Russia annexed from Ukraine ⁠in 2014, in a blow to President Vladimir Putin ahead of ​his meetings ​with US ​and Chinese counterparts ‌on Thursday.
The 19-kilometre (12-mile) bridge is a flagship project inaugurated by Putin in 2018 and a symbol of Russia's attachment to the peninsula.
Earlier this ‌week, Ukrainian drones and ​missiles destroyed the ​central road ​section of the bridge, forcing ‌its main road arch ​to ​crumble into the sea and leaving a yawning gap, according to ​videos ‌and images verified by Reuters.
(Reporting by ​Jekaterīna Golubkova in Tokyo; Editing ​by Bill Berkrot)

item.title: Misbar Tracks Damage to Oil Tanker Dominica Prosperity After Attack off Ras Al Khaimah
item.summary: Satellite Images Show a Plume of Smoke and an Oil Spill. The European Sentinel-2 satellite captured the targeted tanker in several images, with its ...
item.page_text:
Maritime routes in the southern Gulf and around the Strait of Hormuz have witnessed a security escalation over the past few days, with at least three oil tankers targeted in separate incidents. The most notable was an attack on the crude oil tanker Dominica Prosperity off the coast of the Emirate of Ras Al Khaimah. The attack sparked a fire aboard the vessel, and its entire crew was evacuated. The tanker, along with the Fujairah Energy, which was attacked earlier, is linked to South Korean company Sinokor Maritime, according to Reuters, citing maritime risk intelligence provider Marisks. Unknown Projectile Hits Dominica Prosperity off Ras Al Khaimah The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said the tanker was struck at approximately 18:00 UTC on November 11 while stationary and drifting at sea, about 14 nautical miles northwest of Ras Al Khaimah. The agency reported that an unknown projectile struck the engine room and that firefighting operations were ongoing. The incident was detailed in advisory No. 204-26. Maritime intelligence firm Ambrey said the tanker was struck near its stern while exiting the Strait of Hormuz. According to MarineTraffic records, the vessel is a very large crude carrier (VLCC) flying the Liberian flag, with IMO number 9395496. Built in 2011, it measures 330 meters in length and 60 meters in width, with a deadweight tonnage of 297,274. The tanker had been out of signal range for more than 52 days. Its last recorded position was in the northern Indian Ocean near Sri Lanka, as it headed toward the Port of Fujairah. Satellite Images Show a Plume of Smoke and an Oil Spill The European Sentinel-2 satellite captured the targeted tanker in several images, with its recorded dimensions matching those visible in the imagery. The vessel appears off Saqr Port at coordinates 26.01800° N, 55.90057° E. An image captured on November 13 showed a large plume of gray smoke rising from the tanker’s stern, the location of the strike. On November 15, the tanker appeared without any visible smoke, with a small vessel alongside it. Meanwhile, synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images captured by the Sentinel-1 satellite showed a large spill beneath the tanker. The spill covered an area of more than 30 square kilometers and extended along the adjacent coastline. No such spill had been visible in earlier imagery. Three Tankers Targeted Within 48 Hours as Iranian Authority Threatens Sinokor Vessels India’s Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Sarbananda Sonowal, confirmed in a post on X that the UAE Coast Guard had immediately evacuated all 22 crew members aboard the Dominica Prosperity, including 19 Indian nationals, with no casualties reported. He said the tanker was drifting off Saqr Port when it was attacked. The incident followed an attack on the Fujairah Energy, another Liberian-flagged VLCC belonging to the Sinokor fleet, on November 10 while sailing between Ruwais and Dubai . According to the Indian minister, the attack injured four crew members. On November 11, the Saudi tanker NCC Fajr was also struck while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, before the attack on the Dominica Prosperity. No party has claimed responsibility for the attacks, and UKMTO has not identified those responsible. On October 27, an Iranian body known as the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, which Iran says is responsible for the strait, announced through its official X account that Sinokor vessels had recorded the highest number of violations of Iranian transit regulations over the preceding three months. It said enforcement measures had been taken against at least seven of the company's vessels. The authority warned cargo owners, beneficiaries and insurance service providers that, effective November 1, legal action would be taken against all vessels linked to the company, describing it as the largest operator of shuttle trade transporting crude oil through the strait into open waters. Misbar has not verified any connection between these threats and the recent attacks. item.title: Should the USA Give Texas to Russia?
item.summary: Donald Trump's administration is floating the idea that Ukraine should give up the Donbas to Russia in exchange for NATO membership. But how would you feel if it were your country being asked to surrender a fifth of its territory? That's the question posed by Russian Occupation – What if it were your country? , an interactive map that brings the reality of territorial occupation much closer to home. Created by Nini and Levan, a Georgian couple who witnessed the 2008 war in Georgia, the project has a simple but powerful idea: make the scale of Russian occupation tangible by showing it in places that people know. Choose your country and the map highlights an area equivalent to approximately 20% of its territory in red. It provides a hypothetical illustration of what losing a fifth of the country might look like. It's a particularly effective way of communicating the sheer geographical scale of occupation. Rather than looking at an unfamiliar map of eastern Ukraine or the Caucasus, you can see what losing a fifth of your own country might mean. The red area suddenly becomes a collection of familiar places, cities and landscapes. But this is more than a geographical thought experiment.

item.title: IAEA says North Korea is expanding uranium-enrichment plant at Yongbyon - AsiaOne.com
item.summary: A satellite image shows a nuclear material production factory, in Yongbyon, North Korea, May 17. PHOTO: Reuters file. PUBLISHED ON November 19 ...
item.page_text:
VIENNA — North Korea has built an extension to its original uranium-enrichment plant at its Yongbyon nuclear complex as it continues to expand its production of weapons-grade material, UN nuclear watchdog chief Rafael Grossi said on Wednesday (Nov 18).
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has not had access to North Korea since Pyongyang expelled its inspectors in 2009. The agency now observes the country mainly using satellite imagery.
North Korea, formally known as the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), has carried out several nuclear tests and appears to continue to produce the two materials with which one can make the core of a nuclear weapon — highly enriched uranium and plutonium.
"Previously, I have reported to you about the ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon, the construction of an additional enrichment facility at Yongbyon, and the reported further expansion of the DPRK's production of weapons-grade nuclear material," Grossi said in a statement to a quarterly meeting of the IAEA's 35-nation Board of Governors.
Kangson is just outside Pyongyang to the southwest, while the much larger site at Yongbyon is further away from the capital to the north.
"Since mid-September 2026, a further extension to the original Yongbyon enrichment facility has been under construction with the new extension externally complete by late October 2026," he said, without elaborating.
"The ongoing expansion of the DPRK's uranium enrichment programme remains a cause for serious concern," he added.
Grossi said the IAEA has also "observed indications" that the five-megawatt nuclear reactor at Yongbyon that North Korea uses to produce plutonium from spent fuel probably continues to operate and is in its seventh irradiation cycle, after which the spent fuel would be removed for reprocessing.
Another, light-water reactor at Yongbyon has been operating since April of this year, he added.

item.page_text:
Recent satellite imagery has revealed accelerated construction developments at an underground facility near the Shimon Peres Negev Nuclear Research Center (Dimona reactor) in the Negev Desert in southern Israel. The imagery shows a notable expansion of deep excavation work, the construction of underground floors and tunnels, and the emergence of a new structure adjacent to the dome of the old heavy-water reactor. These developments are part of engineering efforts that specialized reports suggest are intended to extend the facility’s operational lifespan and reinforce its nuclear infrastructure against regional missile attacks. Construction Developments Near the Dimona Reactor Satellite imagery confirmed that the newly identified engineering work is concentrated approximately 13 kilometers southeast of the city of Dimona, within the security perimeter of the Dimona nuclear complex, located at the geographical coordinates 30°59'58.07"N 35°8'33.29"E. High-resolution satellite images show a deep excavation site surrounded by thick concrete walls, covering a semi-underground facility consisting of several floors below ground level and connected to new underground access points and tunnels. Nuclear Monitoring Reports and Infrastructure Upgrades These indicators align with the periodic assessment published by the Federation of American Scientists (FAS) in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists on November 10, 2026. The report documented Israel’s continued efforts to modernize its nuclear infrastructure, which is estimated to include approximately 90 nuclear warheads, despite its longstanding policy of nuclear ambiguity. The report, prepared by researchers Hans Kristensen and Mackenzie Knight-Boyle, linked the excavation and tunnel construction work at Dimona to potential efforts to extend the operational lifespan of the aging reactor, which has been operating for decades, with the aim of keeping it functional until 2040. The satellite-documented developments have not been limited to Dimona, as parallel upgrades to underground bunkers and tunnels in the same area had previously been identified. Dimona’s Fortifications Amid Iranian Threats The shift toward deep underground construction and the development of reinforced concrete structures below ground reflect evolving plans to protect strategic facilities, particularly after Dimona was directly targeted by Iranian missiles during the regional confrontations in March. The importance of these engineering fortifications is further underscored by continued public threats from Iran, including statements by Iranian lawmakers and officials in Tehran who warned in October of the possibility of launching military strikes against Dimona facilities if attacks on Iran resume. The disclosure of these construction developments also coincides with heightened local security concerns, reflected in warnings issued by Dimona Mayor Benny Biton on November 17 about an imminent security escalation, amid the U.S. naval buildup in the Middle East. These ongoing developments suggest that concealing sensitive activities deep in the Negev Desert is no longer aimed solely at keeping the nuclear program beyond the reach of international inspections. It has also become a defensive necessity to ensure the operational continuity of Israel’s arsenal in the face of heavy ballistic missiles. item.title: Mangrove forests were "drowning" for decades, but satellite images now show a quiet and ...
item.summary: For decades, scientists watched coastlines shrink — one Landsat frame at a time. The satellite record stretching back to 1984 told a consistent ...
item.page_text:
For decades, scientists watched coastlines shrink — one Landsat frame at a time. The satellite record stretching back to 1984 told a consistent story: mangrove forests were losing ground, swallowed by aquaculture ponds, agriculture, and coastal development . Nearly 1,158 square miles disappeared in less than 30 years.
Then, around 2010, something shifted. A new study published in Science has detected what researchers themselves call an unexpected reversal — a measurable global rebound now visible in the same satellite imagery that once documented only loss.
Scientists have tracked mangrove forests using Landsat satellites since the 1970s, building the longest continuous global record of these ecosystems. For more than three decades, that record told one story: steady, relentless loss . Agriculture, aquaculture, and firewood harvesting chewed through coastal forests across Southeast Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
The numbers were stark. Between 1984 and 2010, nearly 1,158 square miles of mangrove forest vanished from the map.
Then the line changed direction. A new analysis covering 1984 to 2023 — led by Zhen Zhang, an environmental scientist at Tulane University — detected a net gain of nearly 772 square miles since 2010 . Zhang notes this is the first global mangrove mapping effort to span such a long continuous period. The reversal wasn’t predicted. It had to be seen in the data before it could be understood.
Not all of the rebound comes from human effort. About two-thirds of the expansion reflects mangroves naturally colonizing new territory — particularly mudflats formed by sediment deposits near the mouth of the Amazon River and in northern Australia, both of which have seen steady mangrove increases since the 1990s. The remaining third stems from active restoration and regrowth in previously degraded zones .
Temperature is also playing a role at the edges of mangrove range. Warming winters and fewer hard freezes have allowed mangroves in the southeastern United States to push into areas once too cold to support them, Zhang explains. Beyond raw area, canopy density has increased across many regions — especially in South America — signaling forests that aren’t just larger, but healthier.
Few places illustrate the arc of loss and recovery more clearly than Myanmar. Between the 1980s and 2010, the country lost 28.6 percent of its total mangrove area — a rapid unraveling driven by agricultural and aquaculture expansion along its coastlines.
The turnaround began around 2010, driven by several converging forces: heightened awareness following the devastating 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, stronger legal protections for forests, and high sedimentation rates that opened fresh mudflats for colonization . Landsat imagery of Palaw Township in the Myeik District shows the change in visible terms — degraded mangrove forests regenerating in what were once abandoned rice fields. On nearby Pyin Bukyi Island, community-led conservation projects and tree planting have contributed to additional growth.
Since 2010, Myanmar’s mangrove area has grown roughly 10 percent. Meaningful progress — but it recovers only a fraction of what was lost over the preceding three decades.
Mangrove trees are relatively modest in stature, averaging about 42 feet in height. Their ecological impact is something else entirely. These ecosystems store up to four times as much carbon per hectare as taller inland tropical forests, making them among the most carbon-dense environments on Earth.
Their distinctive stilt-like root systems serve two functions at once: buffering coastal communities against erosion and storm surges while providing critical nursery habitat for fish, shrimp, crabs, and other marine species. That combination — carbon sink and coastal shield — places mangrove health at the center of both climate mitigation and adaptation strategies . Losing them costs more than a tree count suggests .
The global picture is improving, but unevenly. Substantial mangrove losses continue in the Niger Delta, pulling down total coverage across West and Central Africa since 2010. In North America and southern Africa, tropical cyclones have caused widespread degradation, wiping out broad sections of forest in short periods.
Zhang is direct about the risk of misreading the data. “The global successes we’ve seen with mangroves during the past decade should not be seen as grounds for complacency,” he cautions. Deforestation remains an active threat even in recovering regions like Myanmar. His study’s broader message is more hopeful: when conservation efforts and reduced deforestation align with natural expansion, the combined effect can be substantial .
The satellite record that once documented only decline now offers something different — evidence that the trajectory can change, and a baseline for watching what comes next. Whether the rebound holds, expands, or stalls will be visible in the same Landsat frames that first revealed the loss.

item.title: A National Digital Twin Brings Infrastructure Education to Pupils across Scotland with CesiumJS
item.summary: Across Scotland, high school pupils are learning about the infrastructure around them through a national digital twin built on CesiumJS . The ...
item.page_text:
Across Scotland, high school pupils are learning about the infrastructure around them through a national digital twin built on CesiumJS. The National Digital Twin of Scotland brings together everything from buildings and power networks to live bus locations, weather, and environmental sensors, all in an intuitive 3D view that gives pupils a way to explore the systems they may one day help design and maintain.
The National Digital Twin of Scotlandâa living, evolving digital representation of infrastructure, environment, and communitiesâbrings real-world learning into the classroom through the GIBE Infrastructure Pathway, an ambitious education initiative connecting schools, universities, and industry through real-world challenges, emerging technologies, and Scotland's infrastructure. Courtesy Tech Unplugged .
The National Digital Twin is being created to complement a new Infrastructure Pathway in Scottish education, which incorporates the Global Infrastructure and Built Environment (GIBE) course. Created by a group of educators, academics, and industry professionals, GIBE has been approved by Scotlandâs qualification authority, with over 50 schools and 600 pupils expected to join for the Academic Year 2027â28.
Primary pupils in the GIBE course learn about wind power by adjusting windspeeds on a fictitious island, Eilean MÃ³r, and measuring the effect on wind turbines; they read graphs to analyze real-time CO2 measurements from around the country.
Pupils can view actual transmission lines and sample a substation from Bentley Systems to learn how energy is distributed across a region. Courtesy Alakbar Zeynalzade.
Secondary school pupils take on even more involved projects. In one unit, they were assigned to design a house that could fit in a courtyard. The pupils visited the real courtyard, took 360-degree images of the location, visualized it in CesiumJS, and measured the space in the digital twin using Cesiumâs measurement tools. The pupils then designed a house and brought the CAD design into their view of the National Digital Twin to check their work and see how it looked on site among the other existing buildings from the Twinâs own drone-scanned photogrammetry, supplemented by Googleâs Photorealistic 3D Tiles. They could even switch on the thermal drone photogrammetry to understand the thermal nature of their site. Finally, they also got to 3D print their houses. With projects like these, pupils engage in a recognizable version of an actual design workflow. Not only are they learning how infrastructure professionals operate, but theyâre working with the digital tools actually used in industry.
Pupils designed houses for a specific space and positioned their design within the National Digital Twin of Scotland in CesiumJS. Then they 3D printed their models. Courtesy Alakbar Zeynalzade.
All of these educational experiences reference the Twin built in CesiumJS . In addition to exploring the natural and built environment with global terrain and satellite imagery, pupils can explore numerous real datasets showing the countryâs infrastructure: photogrammetry created with iTwin Capture Modeler , BIM and CAD content, real-time sensors from across the country, and infrastructure datasets come together in CesiumJS. More than a 3D map, the Twin gives location and context to infrastructure data from across Scotland, bringing static assets, design models, sensor readings, live feeds, and simulations into a common environment.
One of the priorities for the digital twin was that it be lightweight. Scottish pupils have access to Chromebooks and iPads through school, so the application needed to be able to run on their devices. Building on CesiumJS meant the digital twin could provide sophisticated 3D geospatial experiences while running in a browser. With easy-to-manage settings that allow pupils to select how much data is streamed and at what detail, the Twin can even run on pupilsâ phones. That accessibility is what makes national adoption of the Twin possible.
With its flood simulator, the National Digital Twin of Scotland allows pupils to simulate sea level rise. When the water level simulation is combined with Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles, students are able to see the water level compared to each floor of a building. Courtesy National Digital Twin of Scotland. Courtesy Alakbar Zeynalzade.
The National Digital Twin of Scotland and GIBE course were created in a unique collaboration between Heriot-Watt University, the University of Edinburgh and Midlothian Schools, in association with the University of Glasgow. The team consulted closely with industry partners to understand the skills employers need and translate real-world infrastructure challenges into practical classroom projects. Throughout, Bentley Education has supported and advised the team.
Live weather data and forecasts visualize wind speeds while animated wind turbines, representing the countryâs actual wind power system, spin at the appropriate speed. Courtesy Alakbar Zeynalzade.
While educators, universities, Bentley Education, and industry partners all helped shape the initiative, Alakbar Zeynalzade has led the software development of the National Digital Twin, with contributions from university interns. He came to the project with limited GIS experience and no previous experience with Cesium but found support needed to build such an ambitious project.
To bring infrastructure data into your own CesiumJS application, check out our guide to Cesium and BIM/CAD data . To help give pupils in your area access to industry tools for GIS and infrastructure, reach out to Bentley Education .

item.title: Ukraine blew up Putin's bridge using relay drones to bypass Starlink limits - Ars Technica
item.summary: Ukraine's strike used homegrown tech while adapting battlefield lessons from its adversary. ... Vantor satellite image shows multiple smoke ...
item.page_text:
A Ukrainian barrage of missiles and drones collapsed a crucial segment of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s prized Kerch Strait Bridge—and Ukraine’s military pulled off the strike deep within Russian-occupied territory without relying on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications to guide the missiles in.
On the nights of November 15 and November 16, coordinated waves of Ukrainian drones and missiles caused enough damage to collapse one of two steel arches supporting the Kerch bridge’s roadway for automobile traffic, according to an Institute for the Study of War update . Russian sources claimed several hundred Ukrainian drones first overwhelmed Russian air defenses to pave the way for remote-controlled missile strikes focused on the bridge, with the latter prominently including Ukraine’s homegrown Flamingo cruise missile.
The Ukrainian operation adapted a Russian battlefield innovation by using drones equipped with mesh radios to create an airborne communications network, according to the Financial Times . Each networked drone acts as a relay node to extend the communication link between human operators and remotely piloted missiles and strike drones. Russia began using the technique to support long-range drone and missile strikes on Ukrainian cities.
During the Ukrainian attacks on the Kerch Strait Bridge, the flying mesh network allowed operators located more than 250 kilometers away (155 miles) to remotely guide missiles and drones in evading Russian air defenses while also homing in on the bridge’s weakest structural points, according to the Financial Times .
Ukraine’s takedown of the bridge segment was preceded by weeks of preparatory strikes that systematically destroyed or degraded Russian air defense weapons, radars and electronic warfare equipment arrayed to protect the bridge. The November 15 night attack on the bridge also coincided with the largest Ukrainian overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of the full-scale war, Reuters reported .
Notably, Ukraine conducted the coordinated strike with primarily Ukrainian developed or adapted technologies. The Financial Times reported that “Ukrainian units involved in the operation deliberately avoided using Starshield, the military version of Musk’s Starlink satellite network,” because of recent US restrictions that prevent Ukraine from using Starshield on drones or anything else traveling more than 100 miles per hour (161 kilometers per hour).
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the latest US-imposed restrictions on Starshield have not yet been lifted , although SpaceX denied that the restrictions had returned. Zelenskyy described the speed limit as interfering with some Ukrainian drone interceptor technologies that were designed to defend against Russian drones attacking Ukrainian cities and infrastructure .
However, the Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Strait Bridge provide yet another example of how the Ukrainian military and defense technology companies have been learning to fight without relying on Starlink . This is also not the first time that Ukraine, arguably the leading country in developing new battlefield uses of drones , has adopted a Russian battlefield innovation for its own uses.
From Russia’s view, the only glimmer of good news may be that the bridge’s railway section was only moderately damaged. The Ukrainian newspaper Kyiv Independent pointed to Russian news and video sources indicating that trains appeared to be running again on the bridge after the strikes.
But the severe damage to the bridge’s arch and roadway section cuts off a crucial transportation and supply link between Russia and the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula of Ukraine. The Institute for the Study of War assesses that the “destruction of the bridge” will complicate Russia’s ability to maintain its occupation and military basing within the peninsula.
The other overland supply route between Russia and Crimea involves highways running through Russian-occupied southern Ukraine. But Ukrainian forces have already been striking such highway infrastructure and the Russian supply trucks running along the exposed route.
Fallen debris from the bridge’s collapsed arch may also prevent any large ship traffic from passing through the Kerch Strait that connects the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, according to a Telegram channel owner based in Crimea. That makes it even more difficult for Russia to resupply the Crimean peninsula by sea—and Ukrainian drones have previously struck dozens of Russian ships in the Sea of Azov .
Beyond the physical damage to the bridge, such attacks represent a symbolic blow to Putin’s ambition of holding onto the Crimean peninsula. After Russian forces seized Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, Russia based much of its Black Sea Fleet at the naval base in Sevastopol and later used the peninsula as a logistics hub for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The $3.5 billion Kerch Strait Bridge was built as a physical link to cement Russia’s claim over Crimea. Putin personally drove a construction truck across the bridge to commemorate its opening in 2018. He repeated the bridge-crossing feat in a Mercedes in December 2022, after a Ukrainian truck bomb attack temporarily damaged the bridge in October of that year.
In 2025, the bridge was damaged again after Ukraine’s Security Service used agents to plant mines under the bridge supports. Again, Russia repaired the damage.
The Kerch Strait Bridge’s future prospects look much bleaker now following the latest missile and drone strikes. The bridge was initially constructed in two years, and engineering experts told The New York Times that repairs to the bridge roadway could also take two years under normal circumstances. But they also agreed that any damage to the bridge’s piers could extend that repair time—and Russian repair efforts would likely be at risk from future Ukrainian missile and drone attacks.
